chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a large quantity of dried grapes (busr) and takes from it a large quantity of fresh dates (rutab), while the fresh dates are fewer than the dried grapes. He said, 'There is no objection.' I said, 'And if he has a large quantity of dried grapes and takes from it a large quantity of dried dates (tamr), while the dried dates are more than the dried grapes?' He said, 'There is no objection if it is well-known between you two.'

key_terms.بُسْر: Dried grapes (a type of dried fruit)
key_terms.جُلَّة: A large quantity or bulk amount
key_terms.رُطَب: Fresh dates (dates in the rutab stage)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to exchange dried grapes for fresh dates in different quantities according to Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith clarifies the permissibility of *qard* (loan/exchange) involving different stages of dates—busr (drying), rutab (soft), and tamr (ripe)—where quantity may vary based on customary market valuation (*ma'ruf*). It highlights the Shia juristic principle that flexibility in bulk exchanges is granted when the disparity in weight or volume is accepted by local custom, distinguishing it from strict *riba* prohibitions in gold and silver. This ruling underscores the importance of *urf* (custom) in validating commercial transactions within Islamic law.
